title: Pre-completion steps
subtitle: Requisitions, priority searches, the bankruptcy search and getting the money and the deed ready
objectives: Explain the purpose of requisitions on title and what a buyer's solicitor is checking for in the period between exchange and completion
Explain the function of the OS1/OS2 priority search protected by section 72 of the Land Registration Act 2002, and the purpose of a bankruptcy search against an individual buyer or guarantor
Apply the pre-completion checklist — apportionments, redemption statement and TR1 execution — to a transaction and identify the correct next step from a given point in the process

leadingAuthorities.role: Creates the priority period during which a protected official search takes precedence over other applications to register
Set the procedural detail for official searches with priority, including the 30-working-day protection period
Governs registration of pending actions and bankruptcy petitions and orders, searched against an individual's name before completion

leadingAuthorities.citation: Standard Conditions of Sale (5th edn), condition 6.3
leadingAuthorities.role: Governs apportionment of outgoings such as rent, council tax and service charge between seller and buyer as at the completion date

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can list 'searches, requisitions, TR1' as the pre-completion stage without difficulty. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the checklist — this lesson is about knowing what a search protects against, and what happens when it throws up a hit.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well here on recall before. The test pool leans towards fact patterns — an adverse bankruptcy entry, a search about to expire — rather than definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can state what requisitions on title actually check for, and why a priority search exists at all, before moving on to the application-heavy parts.

overview.hook: Contracts are exchanged, the deal is locked in — and yet a buyer's solicitor still has roughly a month of work to do before a single penny changes hands. In that window sits a search that can be defeated by a single missed date, and a name check that has quietly saved more purchases from disaster than almost any other step in the transaction. This lesson is about the unglamorous middle of a conveyance: the period where most of the real risk is actually managed.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The 30-working-day priority period under the Land Registration Act 2002 and Land Registration Rules 2003 is a settled feature of registered conveyancing practice.

parts.heading: Requisitions on title: the last chance to ask questions
parts.voice: structural — explains a routine step precisely
body: Once contracts are exchanged, the buyer's solicitor sends the seller's solicitor a standard set of requisitions on title — formal questions confirming practical completion arrangements that could not sensibly be finalised before exchange: who will hold the keys and when, how the purchase money will be sent (usually by same-day electronic transfer through the banking system used by both firms), what mortgages or charges will be redeemed and undertakings given for their removal, and confirmation of the seller's bank details for the completion monies.

Requisitions are not, by this stage, an opportunity to reopen the substance of the title — that investigation should already be complete before exchange. They exist to nail down the mechanics: exactly how completion itself will happen, hour by hour, so that nothing is left to be worked out on the day.

A buyer's solicitor who skips or rushes requisitions risks discovering, on completion day itself, that a mortgage on the seller's property has not actually been arranged for redemption — a problem that is far easier to solve with two weeks' notice than with two hours.

components.definition: Standard-form questions sent by the buyer's solicitor to the seller's solicitor after exchange, confirming the practical arrangements for completion — keys, funds transfer, redemption of existing mortgages — rather than reopening the substantive title investigation.

interaction.prompt: Is the purpose of requisitions on title to reinvestigate the substance of the seller's title after exchange?
options: No — they confirm the practical mechanics of completion, not the substance of title, which should already be resolved
Yes — requisitions are the buyer's solicitor's main opportunity to raise title defects
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. By the requisitions stage, title has already been investigated and accepted — the questions now are logistical.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Reconsider the timing. Requisitions come after exchange, when the deal is already binding — they are about how completion will run, not whether the title is sound.

parts.heading: The priority search: OS1, OS2, and the 30-working-day shield
parts.voice: case-narrative — explains the mechanism through what it prevents
body: Between exchange and completion, the register can move. Someone else could apply to register an interest against the seller's title — a charge, a notice, even a competing transfer — in the gap before the buyer's own transfer is registered. Left unmanaged, that would let a later-in-time interest jump ahead of a buyer who has already paid for the property.

The solution is the official search with priority: Form OS1 where the buyer is acquiring the whole of a registered title, Form OS2 where only part of the title is being acquired (for example a single plot from a larger registered title). The search does two things at once — it discloses anything recently registered or pending against the title, and, crucially, it creates a priority period of 30 working days under section 72 of the Land Registration Act 2002 and the accompanying Land Registration Rules 2003.

During that 30-working-day window, the buyer's own application to register (submitted with the completed transfer) takes priority over any other application made in the meantime — even one submitted to the Land Registry first — provided the buyer's application is made before the priority period expires. Miss that window, and the protection is simply gone: a later application from someone else can, in principle, leapfrog the buyer's.

components.text: Rules may make provision for priority periods in connection with official searches of the register and may provide that entries made during a priority period take effect subject to the priority conferred by the search, and for the manner in which priority is to operate.
elements: A priority period is conferred by an official search
Applications made within that period take effect with the priority the search confers
The mechanics and length of the period are set out in rules made under the section

interaction.prompt: A buyer's OS1 search is submitted, and the buyer's application to register the transfer is lodged 32 working days later. What is the practical consequence?
options: The priority period has expired, so the buyer's application no longer automatically takes precedence over any intervening entries
Nothing changes — the 30-working-day period is only a guideline with no legal effect
The search itself becomes void and must be repeated regardless of timing
The buyer automatically loses the property to any intervening buyer
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The priority period is a hard limit — once it lapses, an intervening application is no longer automatically defeated by the earlier search.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on what the 30-working-day figure actually is: a protection period, not a mere guideline. Submitting the registration application after it lapses removes the priority the search would otherwise have given.

parts.heading: The bankruptcy search: checking the buyer, not the property
parts.voice: direct — flags a search students often forget is about the client, not the seller
body: Alongside the priority search against the title, a solicitor acting for a lender — and, in practice, for the buyer where a mortgage is involved — must carry out a bankruptcy search against the name of every individual buyer and any guarantor. Unlike the OS1/OS2 search, this is not a search of the registered title at all: it is a search of the register of pending actions and the register of bankruptcy petitions and orders maintained under the Land Charges Act 1972, checked against the individual's name rather than a piece of land.

The reason is straightforward: a lender will not release mortgage funds to, and a solicitor should not allow completion to proceed for, a buyer whose ability to hold and deal with property may be compromised by insolvency. An adverse entry — a bankruptcy petition presented, or an order made — is not automatically fatal to the transaction, but it must be investigated and resolved (for example, shown to relate to a different person of the same name) before completion proceeds.

This search matters just as much for a guarantor as for the buyer themselves: a guarantee is only as good as the guarantor's own solvency, and a lender relying on a compromised guarantor is relying on very little at all.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students sometimes assume the bankruptcy search is checking the seller, on the logic that the seller is the one giving up the property.
components.whyItsWrong: The bankruptcy search protects the lender (and indirectly the buyer) by confirming the buyer or guarantor is entitled to receive mortgage funds and hold the property without an undisclosed insolvency — it has nothing to do with the seller's position, which is addressed by other pre-completion checks.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that should prompt the solicitor to pause and investigate before completion.
interaction.scenarioText: A mortgage-funded purchase is due to complete next week. The OS1 priority search against the title comes back clean. The bankruptcy search against the individual buyer's name discloses a bankruptcy petition presented against a person of the same name three months ago.
tappableSpans: OS1 priority search against the title comes back clean
bankruptcy search against the individual buyer's name
against a person of the same name
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — an adverse bankruptcy entry must be investigated before completion, even though it may ultimately turn out to relate to someone else entirely.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The clean OS1 result is good news about the title, but look at what the bankruptcy search actually disclosed — a petition entry requires investigation regardless of what the title search shows.

parts.heading: Apportionments and the redemption statement
parts.voice: reference-style — works through the money mechanics
body: Where outgoings on a property — ground rent, service charge, council tax paid in advance — straddle the completion date, they are apportioned between seller and buyer so each pays only for their period of ownership. This is dealt with under the standard conditions incorporated into most residential and commercial contracts, and the buyer's solicitor should calculate and agree the figures with the seller's solicitor before completion, so the completion statement is accurate and no separate reconciliation is needed afterwards.

Where the seller has an existing mortgage, the seller's solicitor must obtain a redemption statement from the seller's lender — a figure, valid to a specified date, showing exactly what is needed to discharge the mortgage in full, including any daily interest accruing after that date up to the likely completion date. The seller's solicitor then gives an undertaking to redeem the mortgage from the sale proceeds on completion, which is what allows the buyer's solicitor to proceed with confidence that the property will complete free of that charge.

Getting the redemption figure wrong, or letting it go stale, causes real delay: if completion happens later than the date the statement was calculated to, extra interest will have accrued that the sale proceeds may not cover, and the seller's solicitor will be scrambling to make up a shortfall on the day of completion itself.

components.label: Money items to resolve before completion day
points: Apportioned outgoings (rent, council tax, service charge) agreed between the solicitors
An up-to-date redemption statement obtained from the seller's existing lender
An undertaking from the seller's solicitor to redeem that mortgage from the proceeds on completion
Confirmation of the exact completion monies figure each side expects to send or receive

interaction.prompt: A seller's solicitor obtained a mortgage redemption statement four weeks ago, valid to a date that has now passed, and completion is happening today. What should the seller's solicitor do?
options: Use the original figure regardless, since redemption statements do not change materially over time
Obtain an updated redemption figure before completion, since interest will have continued to accrue since the statement's valid-to date
Ask the buyer's solicitor to cover any shortfall automatically
Proceed to completion and resolve any shortfall with the lender afterwards
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A stale redemption statement risks an accrued-interest shortfall — it should be refreshed so the undertaking to redeem can actually be honoured in full on the day.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Think about what changes over time with a mortgage balance. Daily interest continues to accrue after the statement's valid-to date, so an out-of-date figure risks leaving the redemption short.

parts.heading: Preparing the TR1 for execution
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the practical question before resolving it
body: Here's a question worth pausing on: what actually transfers a registered title from seller to buyer? Not the contract — that only creates an obligation to transfer. The answer is the TR1, the Land Registry's standard form of transfer, executed as a deed by the seller (and by the buyer where the buyer is taking on obligations, such as a restrictive covenant or joint ownership declaration).

In the run-up to completion, the buyer's solicitor drafts the TR1 using the agreed particulars — the parties, the property (by title number), the price, and any special provisions — and sends it to the seller's solicitor for approval and execution in readiness for completion. Because it must be executed as a deed, the formalities are stricter than for an ordinary document: the topic taken up in full in the next lesson, on completion itself.

Getting the TR1 approved and signed in advance — rather than leaving execution to completion day — is what allows the Code for Completion by Post (covered next) to work at all: the seller's solicitor needs to be holding a validly executed transfer, ready to release, at the exact moment completion funds are confirmed as received.

components.label: TR1: what the buyer's solicitor confirms before completion day
points: The TR1 has been drafted with the correct parties, title number, price and any special provisions
The seller's solicitor has approved the draft
The TR1 has been validly executed as a deed and is ready to be held to the buyer's solicitor's order on completion

interaction.prompt: A trainee tells a client that signing the contract at exchange is what transfers legal ownership of the property to them. Is this correct?
options: Yes — exchange of contracts itself transfers legal ownership
No — the contract only creates an obligation to transfer; legal title passes on completion, via the executed TR1 and its registration
Yes, provided the deposit has also been paid
No — legal ownership only ever passes once council tax has been apportioned
interaction.trapExplanation: It is easy to conflate 'binding' with 'transferred' because exchange feels like the decisive moment — but exchange creates an enforceable obligation to complete, while legal title itself only passes through the executed transfer (TR1) and its subsequent registration.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Exchange binds the parties to the transaction; the TR1, executed and registered, is what actually moves legal title.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Separate the two ideas: being bound to a transaction is not the same as legal title having passed. That happens through the executed TR1 and registration, not through exchange.

testPool.prompt: What is the main purpose of requisitions on title, sent after exchange of contracts?
options: To reopen and reinvestigate the substance of the seller's title
To confirm the practical mechanics of completion, such as funds transfer and mortgage redemption
To agree the sale price afresh
To register the buyer's interest at the Land Registry
testPool.explanation: Requisitions confirm logistics — keys, funds, redemption of charges — rather than reopening title, which should already be settled by the time contracts are exchanged.

testPool.prompt: Which Land Registry form is used for an official search with priority where a buyer is acquiring the whole of a registered title?
options: OS1
OS2
TR1
testPool.explanation: OS1 is used for a search against the whole of a registered title; OS2 is its equivalent for a search against part only of a registered title.

testPool.prompt: How long is the priority period conferred by a protected official search under the Land Registration Act 2002 and the Land Registration Rules 2003?
options: 10 working days
20 working days
30 working days
90 calendar days
testPool.explanation: The priority period is 30 working days, within which the buyer's application to register must be lodged to take advantage of the priority the search confers.

testPool.prompt: Against what is a bankruptcy search made, as distinct from an OS1/OS2 priority search?
options: Against the title number of the property
Against the individual name of the buyer or guarantor
Against the seller's solicitor's firm
Against the local authority's planning register
testPool.explanation: The bankruptcy search checks the register of pending actions and bankruptcy petitions and orders against an individual's name, not the property's title — a fundamentally different search from OS1/OS2.

testPool.prompt: A trainee assumes a clean OS1 priority search result means completion can proceed without any further checks on the buyer. Is this a safe assumption?
options: Yes — a clean OS1 result covers every risk relevant to completion
No — the OS1 searches the title, not the buyer; a separate bankruptcy search against the individual buyer or guarantor is still required
Yes, provided the buyer is not taking out a mortgage
No — OS1 results are never reliable and must always be repeated before completion
testPool.trapExplanation: It is easy to treat 'the search came back clean' as a single box ticked, but OS1/OS2 and the bankruptcy search look at entirely different registers for entirely different risks — one is about the title, the other about the individual.
testPool.explanation: A clean title search says nothing about the buyer's or guarantor's own solvency, which is precisely what the separate bankruptcy search is designed to check.

testPool.prompt: A buyer's solicitor submits the OS1 search on day one but does not lodge the application to register the transfer until 35 working days later, believing the priority period is simply a formality with no strict deadline. What is the risk?
options: None — the 30-working-day figure is advisory only and carries no legal consequence
The priority conferred by the search will have lapsed, so an intervening application made in the meantime is no longer automatically defeated
The transfer itself becomes automatically void
The buyer forfeits the deposit paid at exchange
testPool.trapExplanation: Treating the 30-working-day period as a loose administrative guideline rather than a hard statutory protection is the exact mistake this lesson is designed to catch — the priority genuinely lapses once the period runs out.
testPool.explanation: Missing the priority period does not void the transfer itself, but it does strip away the protection against intervening applications that the search was obtained to secure.

testPool.prompt: A bankruptcy search discloses a bankruptcy order made against a name matching the buyer's exactly. The buyer's solicitor is confident it is a different person because the buyer has never been insolvent. What is the correct next step?
options: Proceed to completion, relying on the client's assurance that it must be a different person
Investigate and, if appropriate, obtain evidence (such as further identifying details) confirming the entry relates to a different individual before completion proceeds
Cancel the transaction immediately without further enquiry
Ignore the entry, since bankruptcy searches are not conclusive in any event
testPool.trapExplanation: Relying purely on the client's own assurance is not enough — an adverse entry must be positively investigated and, where it is a false match, properly evidenced as such, not simply assumed away.
testPool.explanation: A matching name is not automatically fatal, but it must be checked and, if it is a false match, documented as such before a lender's solicitor can safely proceed to release funds.

testPool.prompt: A buyer is purchasing a single newly built plot carved out of a larger registered title still owned by the developer for the remaining plots. Which search should the buyer's solicitor use?
options: OS1
OS2
A bankruptcy search only
No priority search is available for part of a title
testPool.explanation: OS2 is used where the buyer is acquiring only part of a registered title, such as a single plot on a development site, rather than the whole title.

testPool.prompt: A seller's mortgage redemption statement was calculated to a valid-to date that has now passed, and completion is taking place today, later than expected. What is the practical risk if the seller's solicitor uses the stale figure without updating it?
options: No risk — mortgage balances never change once a statement is issued
The redemption sent to the lender may fall short, since further daily interest will have accrued since the valid-to date
The buyer will automatically be liable for any shortfall
The Land Registry will refuse to register the transfer
testPool.explanation: Interest continues to accrue on the outstanding mortgage after the statement's valid-to date, so completing later than that date on a stale figure risks a shortfall in the amount needed to redeem the charge in full.

testPool.prompt: A property changes hands mid-way through a period for which the seller has already paid the annual ground rent in advance. How is this normally dealt with before completion?
options: The buyer simply reimburses the seller informally after completion, with no figure agreed in advance
The outgoing is apportioned between seller and buyer as at the completion date and the figure is agreed and included in the completion statement
The seller forfeits the pre-paid amount entirely
The local authority resolves the apportionment automatically
testPool.explanation: Apportionment of outgoings that straddle the completion date is calculated and agreed between the solicitors in advance, so the completion statement is accurate and no further reconciliation is needed.

testPool.prompt: Which document, once executed and registered, actually transfers legal title from seller to buyer — as distinct from the document that merely creates the obligation to do so?
options: The contract signed before exchange
The TR1
The requisitions on title
The redemption statement
testPool.explanation: The contract creates a binding obligation to transfer; it is the TR1, executed as a deed and then registered, that actually passes legal title.

testPool.prompt: Under section 72 of the Land Registration Act 2002, what does the priority period conferred by an official search do?
options: It guarantees the buyer's application will always be approved regardless of any defects
It gives an application made within the period priority over other applications made in the meantime
It extends the completion date automatically
It removes the need to register the transfer at all
testPool.explanation: Section 72 allows rules to confer a priority period so that an application lodged within it takes effect with priority over intervening applications — it does not guarantee approval of a defective application.

testPool.prompt: A search discloses that a third party lodged a competing application against the title one working day after the buyer's OS1 search was made, and the buyer's registration application is lodged 10 working days later, well within the priority period. What is the effect, applying section 72?
options: The buyer's application takes priority over the competing application, despite being lodged later in time
The competing application automatically wins because it was made first
Both applications are automatically rejected
Priority depends entirely on which solicitor phones the Land Registry first
testPool.explanation: This is the entire point of the priority period under section 72: an application made within it takes precedence over an intervening application, even one made earlier in time than the buyer's own registration application.

testPool.prompt: A buyer's solicitor obtains an OS1 search on 1 September but, due to a backlog, does not lodge the registration application until well after the 30-working-day period has expired. A competing charge was registered against the seller's title during that gap. What is the most accurate description of the position?
options: The buyer's application still automatically defeats the competing charge, since the search was obtained first
The priority conferred by the search has lapsed, so the competing charge is not automatically defeated by the buyer's earlier search
The Land Registry will refuse to accept the buyer's application at all
The competing charge is automatically void because it was registered after exchange
testPool.explanation: Once the 30-working-day priority period lapses without the registration application being lodged, the protection against intervening entries is lost — the buyer's application is no longer shielded by the earlier search.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating the pre-completion stage as pure paperwork with no live risk. In fact this is where a stale redemption figure, a missed priority period, or an unresolved bankruptcy hit can each derail completion on the day — the checklist exists precisely because these things are easy to let slip once exchange feels 'done'.
